sections.label: The differences you are making, both big and small

content.text:
During the reporting period, we reached 148 unique people through at least one hub session against a target of 120. Attendance records showed strong demand across age groups, including children, young people, adults and older residents. The largest groups recorded were 53 adults aged 17–64, 42 children aged 8–11 and 39 young people aged 12–16, with a further 11 older residents aged 65+. Our records also showed that 97 of those attending were marked as from low-income households.

We also saw sustained engagement from children and young people. A total of 61 children and young people attended at least three sessions, exceeding the target of 55. Within this group, attendance was split between 28 children aged 8–11 and 33 young people aged 12–16. The attendance tracker provided the evidence for this result.

Young people took an active role in shaping delivery. We recorded 27 young people helping to choose or lead activities against a target of 24. Youth board notes and activity sheets showed that this involvement came mainly from young people aged 12–16, who accounted for , alongside , with .

We built local relationships as part of delivery and worked with more partners than planned. We recorded links with 5 local organisations or groups against a target of . These included a school, food pantry, GP link worker, tenants group and local mosque.

Volunteer involvement grew, although it did not reach the full target during this period. We recruited and supported volunteers against a target of . Volunteer records noted that this figure excluded people who only helped with cooking twice, which helps explain part of the gap between informal support and the counted total.

On wellbeing and connection, reported that they felt less isolated against a target of . Feedback on this measure was mixed in quality rather than direction: only feedback cards were returned, while staff noted that informal chats were much more positive. This suggests that the formal measure may have under-recorded the change participants experienced.

Our learning during the year was clear in two areas. Staff and volunteer notes from March found that the food-first format worked best. We also learned that the formal wellbeing survey had low response rates, which limited how much structured feedback we could gather even where day-to-day conversations suggested positive experiences.

claims.text: We reached 148 unique people through at least one hub session against a target of 120.
Sign-in sheets were used to record attendance, although some names were duplicated where children used nicknames.
Of the 148 people reached, 42 were children aged 8–11, 39 were young people aged 12–16, 53 were adults aged 17–64, and 11 were older residents aged 65+.
The gender breakdown for the 148 people reached was 86 female, 54 male, and 5 non-binary or not said.

assumptions: The submitted records did not include a usable story or quote for this section's outcomes table, so the narrative focuses on measured results and learning notes instead.
Examples of community participation beyond the youth leadership figures were not available in the submitted records for this section.
"What changed" examples suitable for populating every column of the outcomes table were only partly available from monitoring notes, so we summarised them in narrative form.

The submitted records did not include community feedback, and staff or volunteer feedback for "The differences you are making, both big and small". This has been disclosed as a gap rather than estimated.

sections.label: How you are changing what you do

content.text:
During this reporting period, we worked within the first year of delivery. The first progress update covered not reported this period to not reported this period, within a project period running from not reported this period to not reported this period. In line with The National Lottery Community Fund’s reporting requirements, this update reflected on learning from the first year and how that learning informed any changes in our approach.

However, the submitted records did not set out confirmed evidence on changes we made to delivery during the period. They also did not include confirmed information on any planned changes or any support we needed. Because of that, we could not give a verified account here of how learning changed our practice without going beyond the available evidence.

We have therefore kept this section factual and limited to what was evidenced in the records provided. A fuller account of adaptations and next steps would need brief narrative notes from delivery staff on what changed in practice, what was planned next, and whether any support was required.

content.text:
We reported a total budget of £78,500 and actual spend of £78,460 for the year. Overall spend was therefore very close to budget.

Staffing costs were mixed across lines. We spent £29,950 on the part-time project coordinator against a budget of £31,200. We spent £16,480 on sessional youth workers against a budget of £13,600.

Other cost lines also varied. Volunteer training and DBS checks came to £3,140 against a budget of £4,200. Food, heating and room costs were higher than planned at £16,260 against a budget of £13,500. Activity materials and local trips were broadly in line with plan at £7,850 against a budget of £8,000. Evaluation and admin were lower than expected at £4,780 against a budget of £8,000.

The submitted records showed where spend was above or below budget by line item. However, they did not include written explanations for each difference between budget and spend or any separate breakdown between revenue and capital costs within this section.

claims.text: Spend on the part-time project coordinator was £29,950 against a budget of £31,200.
Spend on sessional youth workers was £16,480 against a budget of £13,600.
Spend on volunteer training and DBS checks was £3,140 against a budget of £4,200.
Spend on food, heating and room costs was £16,260 against a budget of £13,500.
Spend on activity materials and local trips was £7,850 against a budget of £8,000.
Spend on evaluation and admin was £4,780 against a budget of £8,000.

assumptions: Written explanations for each difference between budget and spend were not available in the submitted records.
A separate breakdown showing revenue costs compared with capital costs was not available in the submitted records.

The submitted records did not include budgeted total, actual spend total, revenue cost variance, and capital cost variance for "What you spent this year". This has been disclosed as a gap rather than estimated.
